objectives: Contrast two definitions of waste.
Explain the key statistics.
Explain why plastic waste is alarming.
Use not merely … but rather and is predicted to.
content.pedagogy: The opening chapter reframes waste as a design and consumption problem. A two-column organizer (general definition / zero waste definition) and a statistics box help learners process the dense, formal language.
anticipatedMisconceptions: 62 percent is the share of city waste processed in proper facilities, not the share that is recycled.
“Not merely … but rather” does not deny the first idea completely; it says it is not enough.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: not merely … but rather · be predicted to · followed by · participle clauses (each requiring)
Notice (Activity 1): … waste is not merely what is left over, but rather a direct consequence …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *is predicted growing · *followed closely from.
Use (Activity 4): waste as a design problem.
beforeReading: Ask: “Is waste only what is left over?”
duringReading: First reading: How does zero waste define waste?
Second reading: complete the organizer and the statistics box.
Find why plastic waste is alarming.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Organizer and statistics box; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–36 Language Focus 1–3; 36–43 Use: waste as a design problem; 43–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What is the difference between the two definitions?
What do the key statistics show?
Why does each material need its own collection method?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “A Direct Consequence” and “62 Percent” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: consequence, consumption, municipal.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the organizer with the headings written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Rewrite the key statistics as a short news report.

formativeAssessment: Uses not merely … but rather or is predicted to.
expectedResponses: In the context of zero waste, waste is not merely what is left over, but rather a direct consequence of poor product planning. Municipal waste is predicted to grow to 3.8 billion tons by 2050.
content.transferTask: Write about waste as a design problem.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners understand the reframing of waste?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “not merely … but rather”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses not merely … but rather or is predicted to.

objectives: Explain why paper waste management is important.
Describe the paper recycling process.
Describe how wood waste is transformed.
Use prevent … from, the passive and participle clauses.
content.pedagogy: The chapter is written in a formal, impersonal process style. A process flow chart helps learners follow the steps, and learners then write their own process report in the same style.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Paper is compressed for easier transport, not to dry it.
“Disposed of” is a formal way to say “thrown away”.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: prevent + object + from + -ing · passive (are compressed, to be transformed) · participle clause of result (enabling)
Notice (Activity 1): To prevent them from getting wet, …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *prevent them to get wet · *are compress.
Use (Activity 4): a process report.
beforeReading: Ask: “Why do recycling bins have lids?”
duringReading: First reading: Why is paper recycling important?
Second reading: complete the flow chart.
Find what wood waste becomes.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Flow chart; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–36 Language Focus 1–3; 36–43 Use: a process report; 43–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why must paper be kept dry?
Why is paper compressed?
Why is wood an essential material?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Compressed” and “Timber and Boards” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: compressed, obtained, disposed of.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the flow chart with the first step written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write the wood recycling process in formal language.

formativeAssessment: Explains why paper recycling is important.
Uses the passive or prevent … from correctly.
expectedResponses: Paper recycling saves raw materials and brings high economic value. To prevent paper from getting wet, it is collected separately and compressed for easier transportation.
content.transferTask: Write a process report about recycling in your town.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners keep a formal, impersonal style?

rubricLevels.secure: Explains why paper recycling is important.
Uses the passive or prevent … from.

objectives: Explain why plastics cannot all be recycled the same way.
Describe the data on production and waste.
Interpret what happened to plastic waste.
Use participle clauses and either … or.
content.pedagogy: The chapter is a single, data-rich paragraph. Learners turn it into two charts (production vs waste; end-of-life shares) and then interpret, not just describe, the data.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Waste grew faster than production.
Sanitary landfills are controlled; uncontrolled dumps are not.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: participle clauses (rising from … to …) · either … or · be found in · a … percent increase
Notice (Activity 1): … almost doubled, rising from 234 to 460 million tons …
Build (Activities 2–3): complete the data text, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *rose from … to … (as a clause after a comma) · *either … nor.
Use (Activity 4): interpret the data.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Numbers: one hundred fifty-six; three hundred fifty-three million tons; a hundred twenty-six percent.
Stress: LIFE-cy-cle, SAN-i-tar-y, WA-ter-ways.
beforeReading: Ask: “What do you think happens to most plastic waste?”
duringReading: First reading: Why is plastic difficult to recycle?
Second reading: make the two charts.
Find where the remaining 22 percent went.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Two charts; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–36 Language Focus 1–3; 36–43 Use: interpret the data; 43–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did waste grow faster than production?
What is the difference between a sanitary landfill and an uncontrolled dump?
What does the data suggest?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “A 126 Percent Increase” and “Uncontrolled Dumps” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: lifecycle, sanitary landfill, waterways.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the charts with the labels written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short interpretation that ends with a recommendation.

formativeAssessment: Uses participle clauses or either … or.
expectedResponses: Plastic waste rose from 156 to 353 million tons, a 126 percent increase. Only 9 percent was recycled, while 50 percent went to sanitary landfills.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners interpret the data, not only repeat it?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “rising from … to …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses participle clauses or either … or.

objectives: Explain how glass is recycled.
Explain why glass is sorted by color.
Explain why composite packaging is difficult to recycle.
Use reduced relative clauses and once.
content.pedagogy: The chapter contrasts a simple material with a complex one. A comparison table (raw materials · recycling process · difficulty) helps learners build an argument about packaging choices.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Composite packaging layers are bonded with adhesive and must be separated.
“Once” here means “as soon as”, not “one time”.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: reduced relative clauses (designed to …, made by …) · once + clause · to + verb (purpose)
Notice (Activity 1): … advanced facilities designed to break down the adhesive bonds …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *made from combining · *Once that they are sorted.
Use (Activity 4): rethinking packaging.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: LIFE-span, re-MELT-ed, ad-HE-sive, spe-cial-IZED, com-POS-ite.
beforeReading: Ask: “Why is a juice carton harder to recycle than a glass bottle?”
duringReading: First reading: How is glass recycled?
Second reading: complete the comparison table.
Find what advanced facilities do.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Comparison table; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–36 Language Focus 1–3; 36–43 Use: rethinking packaging; 43–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why is glass sorted by color?
What are adhesive bonds?
What happens to composite materials once they are sorted?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Sorted by Color” and “Adhesive Bonds” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: lifespan, remelted, adhesive.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the table with the headings written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short consumer guide on packaging choices.

formativeAssessment: Explains why composite packaging is difficult.
Uses reduced relative clauses or once.
expectedResponses: Glass waste is sorted by color to ensure high-quality, continuous recycling. Composite packaging requires processing in advanced facilities designed to break down the adhesive bonds between its layers.
content.transferTask: Compare glass bottles and juice cartons.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners build an argument from the comparison?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with a reduced relative clause.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses reduced relative clauses or once.

objectives: Explain how metal is produced and recycled.
Explain what vegetable waste oil includes.
Explain why waste oil must be collected separately.
Use once + past participle and protect … from.
content.pedagogy: The chapter presents two materials in formal, compact language. Learners unpack compact forms (once collected) into full clauses and then write a public information leaflet.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Biodiesel is renewable because it comes from plants.
“Once collected” means after collection, not “one time”.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: once + past participle · must be + past participle · protect … from · the general term for
Notice (Activity 1): Once collected, these metals are melted down …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *by processing and purify · *protect water systems of pollution.
Use (Activity 4): a public information leaflet.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: PUR-i-fy-ing, re-COV-er-y, SAF-flow-er, ex-pi-RA-tion, BI-o-die-sel.
beforeReading: Ask: “What happens if you pour cooking oil into the sink?”
duringReading: First reading: How is metal produced?
Second reading: list what counts as vegetable waste oil.
Find what waste oil becomes.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Waste oil list; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–36 Language Focus 1–3; 36–43 Use: a public information leaflet; 43–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: How is metal produced?
What does vegetable waste oil include?
Why is biodiesel described as clean and renewable?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Melted Down” and “Renewable Biodiesel” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: purifying, recovery, expiration date.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the frame: … must be collected separately to …
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short paragraph comparing metal and oil recycling.

formativeAssessment: Uses once or must be correctly.
expectedResponses: Metal waste must be collected separately for recovery. Once collected, it is melted down. Vegetable waste oil must be collected separately to protect water systems from pollution.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners unpack the compact forms correctly?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “Once + past participle”.

objectives: Classify examples of organic waste.
Explain the difference between food loss and food waste.
Interpret the food waste statistics.
Use resulting in, along with and be classified as.
content.pedagogy: This short, data-dense chapter distinguishes food loss (before the customer) from food waste (at house, hospitality or retail level). A food chain diagram with the three figures helps learners see where each happens.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Food “lost post-harvest” happens before it reaches the customer; “wasted” food happens at house, hospitality or retail level.
61 percent is the share of food waste, not of all food.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: resulting in · along with · be classified as · occur in
Notice (Activity 1): …, resulting in both animal and plant-based waste.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *resulting to · *classified like.
Use (Activity 4): a household food policy.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: ag-ri-CUL-tur-al, post-HAR-vest, hos-pi-TAL-i-ty, RE-tail, HOUSE-holds.
beforeReading: Ask: “What is the difference between losing food and wasting food?”
duringReading: First reading: What is organic waste?
Second reading: complete the food chain diagram.
Find where most food waste occurs.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Food chain diagram; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–36 Language Focus 1–3; 36–43 Use: a household food policy; 43–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What is the difference between food loss and food waste?
Why is the household figure important?
Which stage of the food chain can you influence most?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Post-Harvest Loss” and “Households” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: agricultural, post-harvest, retail.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the diagram with the stages written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short news report on food loss and waste.

formativeAssessment: Uses resulting in or be classified as.
expectedResponses: Fruit and vegetable scraps, along with straw, are classified as organic waste. 13.2 percent of food is lost post-harvest, and 61 percent of food waste occurs in households.
content.transferTask: Propose a food waste policy for your household.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners distinguish food loss from food waste?

rubricLevels.secure: Uses resulting in or be classified as.

objectives: Explain how electronic waste is processed.
Explain how batteries work and why they need dedicated bins.
Explain why recycling alone is not enough.
Use while (contrast), allowing … to be and prevent … from.
content.pedagogy: The chapter closes the first part of the book with a turning point: recycling has limits. A benefits / limits table prepares learners for a balanced argument and for the idea of Zero Waste in Chapter 8.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “While” here means “although”, not “at the same time”.
Zero Waste shifts the focus to prevention; it does not reject recycling.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: while (contrast) · allowing + object + to be + past participle · prevent … from + -ing · shift from … to …
Notice (Activity 1): … while recycling processes successfully recover valuable materials, they still require …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *allowing materials be recovered · *prevent chemicals to leak.
Use (Activity 4): the limits of recycling.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: fa-CIL-i-tat-ing, dis-MAN-tled, HAZ-ard-ous, LITH-i-um, CO-balt.
beforeReading: Ask: “If we recycle everything, is the waste problem solved?”
duringReading: First reading: How are electronic waste and batteries processed?
Second reading: complete the benefits / limits table.
Find the shift in focus.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Benefits / limits table; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–36 Language Focus 1–3; 36–43 Use: the limits of recycling; 43–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why must toxic substances be removed safely?
How do batteries work?
Why is recycling alone not enough?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Dismantled” and “Critical Metals” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: facilitating, dismantled, hazardous.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the table with the headings written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short paragraph explaining the shift from managing to preventing waste.

formativeAssessment: Uses while or allowing … to be correctly.
expectedResponses: While recycling recovers valuable materials, it still requires significant energy and effort. So, recycling alone is not enough. Zero Waste shifts our focus from managing waste to preventing it.
content.transferTask: Write a balanced paragraph about recycling.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners present both sides before concluding?

rubricLevels.secure: Uses while or allowing … to be.

objectives: Explain what Zero Waste actually means.
Explain the principle of sustainability.
Explain why discarding resources is a problem.
Use focused on, which means and is recognized as.
content.pedagogy: The chapter corrects a misunderstanding with a question–answer structure and then defines Zero Waste and sustainability. A myth / reality / evidence chart helps learners build a clear explanation.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Zero Waste does not mean producing absolutely no refuse.
Sustainability is about current needs and future generations.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: rhetorical questions · focused on + -ing · which means + -ing · be recognized as
Notice (Activity 1): So, what does ‘zero waste’ actually mean?
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *focused in · *which means to meet · *recognized like.
Use (Activity 4): a Zero Waste mindset.
beforeReading: Ask: “What does zero waste actually mean?”
duringReading: First reading: What does Zero Waste actually mean?
Second reading: complete the myth / reality / evidence chart.
Find what zero waste is recognized as.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Myth / reality / evidence chart; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–36 Language Focus 1–3; 36–43 Use: a Zero Waste mindset; 43–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why is producing absolutely no refuse impossible?
What is sustainability?
What does this ongoing pollution threaten?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “A Sustainable Approach” and “An Essential Bridge” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: refuse, mindset, accelerates.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with the myth written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short definition of Zero Waste for a dictionary.

formativeAssessment: Uses focused on or which means correctly.
expectedResponses: Zero Waste is a sustainable approach focused on using resources smartly and minimizing waste. It is based on sustainability, which means meeting our current needs without damaging the resources of future generations.
content.transferTask: Explain the Zero Waste mindset to a skeptical friend.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners correct the myth with evidence?

rubricLevels.secure: Uses focused on or which means.

objectives: Explain the circular economy and its objective.
Explain why it is called circular.
Contrast the circular and the linear economy.
Use no longer, at the expense of and which-clauses.
content.pedagogy: The chapter defines the circular economy by analogy (nature) and by contrast (the linear economy). A line-and-loop diagram makes the contrast visual and supports a contrast paragraph.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The circular economy does not stop growth; it stops growth from harming nature.
“At the expense of” means causing harm to something.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: no longer · at the expense of · non-defining which-clauses · instead of + -ing
Notice (Activity 1): … economic growth no longer comes at the expense of nature.
Build (Activities 2–3): sort the descriptions, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *not longer · *at the expenses of.
Use (Activity 4): two economies.
beforeReading: Ask: “What happens to a phone after you stop using it?”
duringReading: First reading: What is the circular economy?
Second reading: draw the line and the loop.
Find the main objective.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Line-and-loop diagram; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–36 Language Focus 1–3; 36–43 Use: two economies; 43–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why is it called circular?
How does it work like nature?
What is the main objective?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “A Continuous Loop” and “Take-Make-Waste” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: eliminate, objective, at the expense of.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the line-and-loop diagram with the first steps written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short contrast of the two economies.

formativeAssessment: Uses no longer or at the expense of correctly.
expectedResponses: The circular economy aims to eliminate waste and pollution by keeping products in use for as long as possible. Its main objective is to ensure economic growth no longer comes at the expense of nature.
content.transferTask: Contrast a smartphone in the two economies.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners use clear contrast language?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “at the expense of”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses no longer or at the expense of.

objectives: Explain the three principles in detail.
Explain designing for longevity.
Explain the difference between recycling and upcycling.
Use academic verbs and can be achieved by.
content.pedagogy: The chapter uses academic verbs (focus on, address, seek to, involve, target). Learners notice the verb patterns and use them in a design brief that applies the principles.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Reduce prevents waste at the source; recycling deals with waste after it exists.
Upcycling creates higher value; recycling creates new materials.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: focus on + -ing · seek to + verb · involve + -ing · can be achieved by + -ing · place emphasis on
Notice (Activity 1): This can be achieved by collecting and recycling waste …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *focus on prevent · *seeks keeping · *involves to convert.
Use (Activity 4): a design brief.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: in-TEN-tion-al-ly, lon-GEV-i-ty, up-GRADE (verb), UP-cy-cling, em-PHA-sis.
beforeReading: Ask: “Why do some products last for decades and others only months?”
duringReading: First reading: What are the three principles?
Second reading: list the verbs that introduce each principle.
Find how longevity can be achieved.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Principles table; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–36 Language Focus 1–3; 36–43 Use: a design brief; 43–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why is Reduce about the source?
How can products be designed for longevity?
How is upcycling different from recycling?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Preventing Waste at the Source” and “Higher Value” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: intentionally, longevity, upgrade.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give a table with the three principles and their verbs.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short guide to the three principles using three academic verbs.

expectedResponses: The principle of Reduce focuses on preventing waste at the source. Products should be made more durable, easy to repair and simple to upgrade. Upcycling targets transforming waste into products of higher value.
content.transferTask: Write a design brief for a product built for longevity.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners use the academic verbs with the correct patterns?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “can be achieved by …-ing”.

rubricLevels.notYet: Point to the Reuse and Repair paragraph.

content.chapter: Chapter 11: Why Is the Circular Economy Important?
objectives: Explain the three key benefits.
Explain how efficiency is achieved.
Evaluate the potential of the circular economy.
Use has the potential to, while + -ing and increasingly.
content.pedagogy: The chapter is structured as benefits plus a cautious conclusion. Learners notice the hedging (has the potential to) and write an evaluation that includes a limit.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “Has the potential to” does not mean it is certain.
Efficiency means minimizing use and maximizing reuse at the same time.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: has the potential to · while + -ing · increasingly + adjective · by + -ing
Notice (Activity 1): It has the potential to reduce waste …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *has the potential of reduce · *an increasing important role.
Use (Activity 4): evaluate the benefits.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: U-ti-liz-ing, ef-FI-cient-ly, dis-POS-al, po-TEN-tial, in-CREAS-ing-ly.
beforeReading: Ask: “Who benefits from the circular economy?”
duringReading: First reading: What are the three benefits?
Second reading: complete the benefit chart.
Find how the writer hedges.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Benefit chart; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–36 Language Focus 1–3; 36–43 Use: evaluate the benefits; 43–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: How does the circular economy reduce waste?
How is efficiency achieved?
Why does the writer say “has the potential to”?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Utilizing Resources” and “Increasingly Important” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: utilizing, disposal, potential.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with the three headings written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short evaluation with a benefit and a limit.

formativeAssessment: Uses has the potential to or while + -ing.
expectedResponses: The circular economy reduces waste, uses resources more efficiently and supports sustainable growth. It has the potential to lower pollution, and it will play an increasingly important role.
content.transferTask: Evaluate which benefit matters most for your country.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners include a limit in their evaluation?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “has the potential to”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses has the potential to or while + -ing.

objectives: Explain how waste contributes to the climate crisis.
Explain how better waste management can cut emissions.
Explain the injustice of climate impacts.
Use making …, yet, due to and furthermore.
content.pedagogy: The chapter builds a formal argument that links waste and climate and raises a question of justice. An argument map (cause → effect → solution → injustice) prepares learners for their own argument.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Methane comes from organic materials rotting in landfills.
Developing countries have low emissions but suffer the most.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: making + object + noun (result) · due to · yet · furthermore · present perfect (have more than doubled)
Notice (Activity 1): …, yet they often suffer the most …
Build (Activities 2–3): fill the linkers, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *Due to consumers consume · *Yet, but …
Use (Activity 4): climate justice.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: PO-tent, METH-ane, in-JUS-tice, POL-lu-tants, AT-mos-phere.
beforeReading: Ask: “Is it fair that some countries suffer more from climate change?”
duringReading: First reading: How is waste linked to the climate crisis?
Second reading: complete the argument map.
Find the injustice.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Argument map; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–36 Language Focus 1–3; 36–43 Use: climate justice; 43–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why is methane a problem?
How can Zero Waste prevent emissions at the source?
Why is the situation unjust?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Potent Methane” and “A Major Injustice” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: potent, trend, injustice.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the argument map with the first box written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short summary of the chapter’s argument.

formativeAssessment: Explains the link between waste and climate.
expectedResponses: Organic materials release potent methane when they rot in landfills. Better waste management could cut emissions by 15 to 20 percent. Many developing countries have low emissions, yet they suffer the most.
content.transferTask: Write an argument about climate justice.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners build a reasoned argument?

rubricLevels.secure: Explains the link between waste and climate.

objectives: Explain why action before waste is generated is essential.
Explain how food waste can be minimized.
Explain how single-use packaging can be replaced.
Use can be minimized through, similarly and be swapped for.
content.pedagogy: The chapter moves from principle to practice. A problem–means–alternative table (problem · how to minimize · waste-free alternative) helps learners plan a formal proposal.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “Swap A for B” means you give up A and take B.
The chapter says most single-use packaging, not all, is unnecessary.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: can be minimized through · similarly · be swapped for · prevent + -ing
Notice (Activity 1): Food waste can be minimized through proper training …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *minimized throughout · *swapped to alternatives.
Use (Activity 4): a proposal for the school.
beforeReading: Ask: “Which single-use items do you use every week?”
duringReading: First reading: What is the best kind of waste?
Second reading: complete the problem–means–alternative table.
Find four items that can be swapped.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Problem–means–alternative table; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–36 Language Focus 1–3; 36–43 Use: a proposal for the school; 43–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why is it essential to act before waste is generated?
Where can food waste be minimized?
How can single-use packaging be replaced?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Never Created at All” and “Waste-Free Alternatives” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: generated, disposable, alternatives.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the table with the problems written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short leaflet of practical suggestions.

formativeAssessment: Explains acting before waste is generated.
Uses can be minimized through or be swapped for.
expectedResponses: The best kind of waste is the one that is never created at all. Food waste can be minimized through proper training and better buying policies. Disposable water bottles can be swapped for waste-free alternatives.
content.transferTask: Write a proposal to reduce waste in your school canteen.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners write realistic, formal proposals?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “can be swapped for”.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains acting before waste is generated.
Uses can be minimized through or be swapped for.

content.chapter: Chapter 14: Cities, Families and the Future
objectives: Explain the role of local governments.
Explain why educating children and families is effective.
Explain why Zero Waste is an ongoing journey.
Use rather than, not … but and since.
content.pedagogy: The closing chapter moves from city policy to personal mindset and ends with Gandhi’s insight. The council debate brings the whole book together and asks learners to prioritize and justify policies.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “Since” here means “because”, not “from a time”.
Gandhi’s words compare need and greed; they do not say resources are lacking.

metadata.title: Zero Waste B2 — Teacher’s Book
metadata.subtitle: Our World Today
metadata.estimatedDuration: 14 chapter units of 45 minutes each. Whole-book review pages follow separately.
metadata.targetLearners: Learners who can follow extended informational texts about society, economy and the environment, and who can produce clear, detailed explanations, evaluations and arguments.
metadata.purpose: Develop evidence-based B2 reading, listening, speaking and writing through an extended informational text about waste and Zero Waste: waste data and recycling processes, the limits of recycling, sustainability, the circular economy, the three principles and their benefits, waste and the climate crisis, and the roles of people, families and cities, using the Language Focus attached to every chapter.
metadata.approachDesc: Every chapter follows the TYMM route. YDAB1 listening and YDAB2 reading establish meaning and evidence; the Quick Challenge checks comprehension. Grammar is then learned inductively: in the Language Focus, learners first NOTICE a form in a real chapter sentence and work out what it does, then BUILD it in controlled, meaningful practice, and finally USE it in connected YDAB3 speaking and YDAB4 writing about their own world. At B2, learners also notice how the writer signals certainty (is predicted to / has the potential to / could) and builds a formal argument (not merely … but rather / yet / furthermore / rather than), and they use these forms in their own writing.
metadata.assessmentEvidence: 14 Quick Challenges, text-evidence checks, chapter Language Focus tasks (Notice → Build → Use), exit tickets, Knowledge Check, Vocabulary Challenge, Language Review and Final Challenge.

formative: Short spoken and written Use tasks

readingFramework.before: Activate only what the chapter needs: a short question, a real object, a chart or a link to the previous chapter.
readingFramework.during: Listen first for gist (when the audio is ready), then read and follow the chapter’s own structure: a definition organizer, a process flow chart, data charts, a comparison table, a food chain diagram, a benefits / limits table, a myth / reality chart, a line and a loop, an argument map or a list of policies.
readingFramework.after: Complete the Quick Challenge, then the chapter’s Language Focus (notice → build → use), then a connected B2 transfer: an explanation, proposal, evaluation or argument about the learners’ own world.

vocabularyApproach.selection: Word Notes are the bold words of the teacher-approved text. Prioritize them and the words needed for the chapter’s key idea.
vocabularyApproach.method: Infer meaning from context, a real object or a picture before any direct explanation.
vocabularyApproach.recycling: Reuse vocabulary in Language Focus tasks, exit tickets, Key Terms and the Language Review.

metadata.grammarApproach: Inductive and text-based. Start from the chapter sentence, ask a meaning question (What does this form tell us? How certain is the writer?), let learners formulate the rule, then confirm it and practice it in context. B2 targets include reduced relative and participle clauses, prevent … from, academic verb patterns, hedging, formal contrast linkers and rather than / not … but. Rule explanations appear in the app only after learners answer.
grammarSequence: Ch1: not merely … but rather · be predicted to · followed by · participle clauses (each requiring)
Ch2: prevent + object + from + -ing · passive (are compressed, to be transformed) · participle clause of result (enabling)
Ch3: participle clauses (rising from … to …) · either … or · be found in · a … percent increase
Ch4: reduced relative clauses (designed to …, made by …) · once + clause · to + verb (purpose)
Ch5: once + past participle · must be + past participle · protect … from · the general term for
Ch6: resulting in · along with · be classified as · occur in
Ch7: while (contrast) · allowing + object + to be + past participle · prevent … from + -ing · shift from … to …
Ch8: rhetorical questions · focused on + -ing · which means + -ing · be recognized as
Ch9: no longer · at the expense of · non-defining which-clauses · instead of + -ing
Ch10: focus on + -ing · seek to + verb · involve + -ing · can be achieved by + -ing · place emphasis on
Ch11: has the potential to · while + -ing · increasingly + adjective · by + -ing
Ch12: making + object + noun (result) · due to · yet · furthermore · present perfect (have more than doubled)
Ch13: can be minimized through · similarly · be swapped for · prevent + -ing
Ch14: rather than · not … but · since (reason) · there is no better … than

skillsFocus.listening: TYMM YDAB1: follow extended narration for gist, data, processes and arguments.
skillsFocus.reading: TYMM YDAB2: identify arguments, degrees of certainty, data, causes, results and policy details.
skillsFocus.speaking: TYMM YDAB3: explain and evaluate ideas, propose policies and present balanced positions.
skillsFocus.writing: TYMM YDAB4: produce clear, detailed B2 paragraphs and short arguments with evidence, hedging and balanced conclusions.

valuesFocus: D16 Responsibility — Caring for nature and future generations.
D5 Sensitivity — Noticing what nature needs.
D20 Helpfulness — Sharing resources in a community.
languageFocus: Every one of the 14 chapters has a Language Focus set built as Notice → Build → Use (4 activities).
Use the Language Focus after basic comprehension and the Quick Challenge.
Always start from the story sentence and ask a meaning question before naming the form.
The Use step is connected spoken or written production about a new, non-story situation.
metadata.differentiationNotes: Reduce linguistic load without lowering the reasoning target: one paragraph at a time, long sentences unpacked, charts given in part, selected vocabulary, audio replay, sentence frames and oral rehearsal. Extend by asking for evaluation, counterpoints and evidence from more than one chapter, not by introducing outside facts.

sensitiveNotes.title: Source fidelity and respectful teaching
notes: Keep explanations within the wording of the book; do not add outside numbers or opinions.
Talk about food waste and money with care; some families may have little food at home.
Do not let learners touch real batteries or broken electronics in class; use pictures or closed, clean objects.

globalCitizenship.title: Global Citizenship and Cultural Bridges
globalCitizenship.description: Zero Waste connects with questions every community faces today: how to use less, how to share and repair, and how to protect nature together.

themes.title: Need and greed:
themes.description: Gandhi said the world has enough for everyone’s need, but not for everyone’s greed (Chapter 14). Discuss overconsumption in different cultures.

themes.title: Climate justice:
themes.description: Developing countries have low emissions, yet they often suffer the most (Chapter 12). Discuss how responsibility should be shared.

themes.title: Sharing:
themes.description: Tool libraries and material banks prevent waste locally (Chapter 14). Discuss sharing traditions in your community.

themes.title: Future generations:
themes.description: Sustainability protects the resources that future generations will need (Chapter 8). Discuss what we owe to people in the future.

miniProject.title: Zero Waste: A City Council Debate
miniProject.desc: In groups, each member becomes an analyst for part of the book: materials, concepts, impact or policy. Prepare a two-minute statement with one quotation, debate and agree on three policies.

reflectivePrompt.title: A Policy Argument
reflectivePrompt.desc: Most single-use packaging is actually unnecessary (Chapter 13). Write eight to ten sentences arguing whether your city should ban single-use plastics. Use evidence from the book and one counterpoint.

valuesEducation.title: TYMM Values in Action
valuesEducation.description: Use only values the chapter really shows. Ask for the sentence first, then connect the value to a small action learners can do and see. See https://tymm.meb.gov.tr/beceriler/erdem-deger-eylem-cercevesi.

items.label: D16 Responsibility
items.value: Responsibility: Sustainability means meeting our current needs without damaging the resources that future generations will need (Chapter 8).

items.label: D5 Sensitivity
items.value: Sensitivity: Waste batteries must be collected in dedicated bins to prevent hazardous chemicals from leaking into the soil and water (Chapter 7).

items.label: D20 Helpfulness
items.value: Helpfulness: Cities can set up tool libraries or material banks to prevent waste locally (Chapter 14).

items.label: D1 Justice
items.value: Justice: Many developing countries have very low emission levels, yet they often suffer the most from climate impacts (Chapter 12).

cefrProfile.intro: This book is written for CEFR B2. The table links the B2 descriptors of the End-of-Level Test B2 to the chapters of this book where learners practice them.

rows.descriptor: Can read with a large degree of independence, adapting style and speed of reading to different texts and purposes, and using appropriate reference sources selectively.
practice: Chapter 3 (Plastic): Interpret the data on plastic waste.
Whole book: Knowledge Check and Final Challenge.

rows.descriptor: Can write clear, detailed texts on a variety of subjects related to his field of interest, synthesising and evaluating information and arguments from a number of sources.
practice: Chapter 7 (Electronic Waste and Batteries): Write a balanced paragraph on the limits of recycling.
Chapter 12 (Waste and Climate): Write an argument about climate justice.
Language Review, “Use: A Policy Argument”: Write an argument with evidence and a counterpoint.

rows.descriptor: Can give clear, systematically developed descriptions and presentations, with appropriate highlighting of significant points, and relevant supporting detail.

Chapter 14 (Cities, Families and the Future): Present your analyst statement in the council debate.

test.title: End-of-Level Test B2
test.when: Give the test when the class has finished the B2 books it reads this term. It has four parts and takes about 85 minutes plus a short speaking test for each learner.
parts: Reading and Language (50 minutes): in the app. The learner gets a test code at the end.
Writing (35 minutes): on paper. Write an essay discussing this statement: “Travel teaches us more than books do.” (180–220 words)
Speaking (about 10 minutes): one learner with the teacher, in 3 parts.
Scoring: type the test code in “Score a test”, then score Writing and Speaking with the bands. Copy the pilot line for the pilot results sheet.

metadata.title: Zero Waste B2 — Self-Study Guide
metadata.subtitle: Read • Find • Check • Build • Use
metadata.estimatedStudyTime: About 30 minutes per chapter, plus the review pages at the end
metadata.whoIsThisFor: B2 learners who study the text about Zero Waste alone or with a teacher.
learningGoals: Understand the 14 chapters of Zero Waste.
Find evidence in the text before answering.
Follow the argument of the Zero Waste text from waste data to policy.
Evaluate Zero Waste, the circular economy and climate justice with evidence from the book.
Use each chapter’s Language Focus in connected sentences.
recommendedUse: Study one chapter at a time.
Read (and listen, when the audio is ready) before the Quick Challenge.
Repair wrong answers with the text.
Do the Language Focus after you understand the chapter.
Do the review pages after Chapter 14.

readingDiary.intro: Keep this diary when you finish the book. Write short answers.
prompts: The date I finished the book:
My favorite chapter, and one reason:
One idea about waste that I think matters most for my community, and why:
One sentence for a friend: “Read this book because …”
One new word I want to keep:
The next book I want to read in the library:

sections.title: 1. Make Your Plan
sections.text: This book has 14 chapters. Plan the whole book before Chapter 1.
points: Choose your study days and how many chapters you will read each week.
Write one personal goal for this book.
Save new words to My words and review them after one day, three days and one week.

sections.title: 2. One Chapter per Session
sections.text: Each chapter takes about 30 minutes. Open “Study Path” for the steps of your chapter.
points: Preview the title and the “Before You Read” question.
Read for the main idea.
Find the evidence.
Do the Quick Challenge.
Do the Language Focus.

sections.title: 3. Read and Listen
sections.text: Read every chapter twice: once for the main idea, once for the details. When the audio is ready, listen once while you follow the text.
points: First reading: What is the chapter about?
Second reading: Mark names, dates and linking words.
Say one long sentence aloud with the right pauses.

sections.title: 4. Word Notes
sections.text: Bold words have Word Notes. Use them after you have tried to understand the sentence yourself.
points: Guess the meaning from the sentence.
Check the Word Note.
Write the word in a new sentence of your own.

sections.title: 5. Quick Challenge
sections.text: Answer before you read the feedback. If you are wrong, repair the answer with the text.
points: Find the paragraph the question is about.
Read the key sentence again.
Explain why the right answer is right, then try again.

sections.title: 6. Language Focus
sections.text: Each chapter has 4 Language Focus activities built from the chapter’s own sentences.
points: Activity 1 (Notice): Look at a sentence and what it means.
Activities 2–3 (Build): Choose, complete, correct or rewrite forms.
Activity 4 (Use): Write or say connected sentences about a different situation.

sections.title: 7. When It Is Hard
sections.text: Some chapters have many names and dates. Change how you study, not your goal.
points: Read one paragraph only.
Make a time line of the dates.
List the names and what each one did.
Learn only three words today.

sections.title: 8. Values in the Book
sections.text: The book shows responsibility, sensitivity, helpfulness and justice. Find the sentence first, then think of a small action of your own.
points: Responsibility: Responsibility: Sustainability means meeting our current needs without damaging the resources that future generations will need (Chapter 8).
Sensitivity: Sensitivity: Waste batteries must be collected in dedicated bins to prevent hazardous chemicals from leaking into the soil and water (Chapter 7).
Helpfulness: Helpfulness: Cities can set up tool libraries or material banks to prevent waste locally (Chapter 14).
Justice: Justice: Many developing countries have very low emission levels, yet they often suffer the most from climate impacts (Chapter 12).

sections.title: 9. At the End of the Book
sections.text: After Chapter 14, do the review pages in this order. Go back to a chapter when an answer is not clear.
points: Key Facts
Knowledge Check
Vocabulary Challenge
Master Glossary
Key Terms
Language Review
Final Challenge

sections.title: 10. Look Back
sections.text: Before Chapter 1 and again at the end, answer the “I can” statements of a few chapters. What can you do now that you could not do before?
points: Which chapter changed what you knew?
Explain to someone at home in six sentences what Zero Waste means and why it matters, in your home language or in English.
